title: What Happens If AI Becomes Smarter Than Humans?

shots.vo: For as long as humans have existed, we've been the smartest thing on the planet. That's how a fairly weak, slow animal ended up shaping the entire world.
But what happens if we build something smarter than us? Not just better at chess, or math, but better at everything?
Some of the world's leading scientists think this could happen within our lifetimes. Others think it's decades away, or may never happen at all. So what would it actually mean?

Researchers call this artificial general intelligence, or AGI: a machine that can learn and do almost any mental task a human can. Go beyond that, and you get what's called superintelligence, something smarter than the smartest humans in every field.

The question is old. In 1950, the mathematician Alan Turing asked, can machines think? He proposed a test: if a machine could hold a conversation you couldn't tell apart from a human's, maybe we should say it thinks.
Let's start with how we got here. In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. But Deep Blue couldn't do anything except play chess.
In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol at Go, a game with more possible positions than there are atoms in the observable universe.
In the second game, it played a move so unusual that experts first thought it was a mistake. Move thirty-seven turned out to be brilliant. The machine had found an idea no human had seen.
Then AI started doing science. DeepMind's AlphaFold predicted the 3D shapes of hundreds of millions of proteins, a problem biologists had struggled with for fifty years.

params.sub: plus the Nobel Prize in Physics for neural-network pioneers

shots.vo: In 2024, that work shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The same year, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to pioneers of the neural networks behind modern AI.
And today, large language models can write code, explain science, and pass difficult professional exams. They're trained on huge amounts of text, using enormous data centers.

Under the hood, a language model is trained to do one thing: predict the next word. It reads trillions of words, and adjusts billions of internal numbers, until it gets very good at that. Along the way, it picks up grammar, facts, and patterns of reasoning.
But there's a big difference between these systems and true general intelligence. Today's AI can be brilliant at some tasks, and surprisingly bad at others.

It can make confident mistakes, struggle with reliable long-term planning, and doesn't learn from experience the way we do. Researchers call the goal artificial general intelligence, or AGI: a system that can learn and do almost any task a human can.
Your brain runs on about twenty watts of power, roughly the same as a dim light bulb. But computers have one big advantage. They can be scaled up.
The amount of computing power used to train the most advanced AI models has been growing about four to five times every single year. That's one reason progress has felt so sudden.

Researchers discovered something surprising, called scaling laws. Make the models bigger, give them more data and more computing power, and they improve in a fairly predictable way. That's why companies are building enormous data centers.

params.sub2: that machines can do every task better than humans

shots.vo: So when could AI match us? In a large survey of almost three thousand AI researchers, published in 2024, the combined forecast gave a fifty percent chance by 2047 that machines could outperform humans at every task.

params.sub: forecasts range from a few years to never

shots.vo: But individual answers ranged from just a few years to more than a century. And those forecasts have shifted a lot as the technology has improved. The honest answer is that nobody knows.
Back in 1965, the mathematician I. J. Good, who had worked with Alan Turing, described a striking idea. An ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines.

Those machines could design better ones still, in a runaway loop that some call an intelligence explosion. Good wrote that the first ultraintelligent machine would be the last invention humanity ever needed to make.
Whether that could really happen is hotly debated. There may be hard limits on computing power, energy, data, and how fast experiments can be run in the real world.

And even without an explosion, digital minds have strange advantages. Once trained, an AI can be copied thousands of times, run day and night, and share what it learns instantly. No human expert can do that.
If it goes well, the upside could be enormous. Imagine millions of tireless digital scientists working on cancer, new materials, clean energy, and diseases we've given up on.
AlphaFold is a small glimpse of that. Discoveries that once took a career could take days. Some researchers think AI could help compress decades of scientific progress into a few years.
So what's the worry? One of the biggest is called the alignment problem: making sure a powerful AI actually does what we intend, not just what we literally told it.

Here's a real example. In 2016, researchers trained an AI to play a boat racing game, rewarding it for points. Instead of finishing the race, it found a spot where it could circle forever, hitting the same targets and racking up points.

That's funny in a video game. It's less funny in a system running power grids, financial markets, or weapons. It's the King Midas problem. He got exactly what he asked for, and everything he touched turned to gold.

And it gets trickier as systems get smarter. A capable AI pursuing almost any goal might learn that being switched off would stop it reaching that goal. Researchers are studying how to build systems that reliably accept correction.

This isn't only theory. In controlled tests in 2024, researchers found that some advanced models would occasionally mislead their testers, or try to avoid being retrained, when placed in scenarios designed to tempt them.

There's also misuse: people using powerful AI for cyberattacks, scams, or designing dangerous weapons. And there's the question of power. Whoever controls the most capable AI could gain enormous influence over everyone else.
Then there's work. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund estimated that around forty percent of jobs worldwide are exposed to AI. Some will be helped by it. Others could be replaced.

We've been here before. Machines replaced many farm and factory jobs, and new kinds of work appeared. The difference is that a truly general AI could, in principle, do almost any task, including the new ones.

lines: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI
should be a global priority alongside
params.sub: — statement signed by hundreds of AI researchers and leaders

shots.vo: These concerns aren't coming only from outsiders. In 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and tech leaders signed a one-sentence statement saying that reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority.

params.sub: median chance researchers gave of an extremely bad outcome
params.sub2: such as human extinction — the same 2024 survey

shots.vo: In that same large survey, the typical researcher put the chance of an extremely bad outcome, like human extinction, at around five percent. That's not likely, but it's far too high to ignore.

Other experts think these fears are overblown. They argue that today's systems are far from true understanding, and that we'll have plenty of time to spot problems and fix them as the technology improves.
Either way, work on safety is growing. Researchers are trying to look inside neural networks to understand how they reach their answers. It's called interpretability.
Companies and governments now test advanced models for dangerous abilities before release, and train them using human feedback to be more helpful and honest.
And laws are arriving. The European Union passed the world's first broad AI law in 2024, and many countries have signed agreements to cooperate on AI safety.

In 2023, world leaders met at Bletchley Park in England, where codebreakers once worked during World War Two. Twenty-eight countries and the European Union signed a declaration on the risks of the most powerful AI.

So what happens if AI becomes smarter than humans? The truth is, it depends on choices we make now: how carefully we build it, who controls it, and whether we keep humans in charge of the decisions that matter.

vo: It could be the most important invention in our history. The question is whether we'll be ready for it.
